section_title: How does the conflict with Ephraim turn deadly?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 Then the men of Ephraim assembled and crossed the Jordan to Zaphon. They said to Jephthah, “Why have you crossed over to fight the Ammonites without calling us to go with you? We will burn your house down with you inside!” 2 But Jephthah replied, “My people and I had a serious conflict with the Ammonites, and when I called, you did not save me out of their hands. 3 When I saw that you would not save me, I risked my life and crossed over to the Ammonites, and the LORD delivered them into my hand. Why then have you come today to fight against me?”

4 Jephthah then gathered all the men of Gilead and fought against Ephraim. And the men of Gilead struck them down because the Ephraimites had said, “You Gileadites are fugitives in Ephraim, living in the territories of Ephraim and Manasseh.” 5 The Gileadites captured the fords of the Jordan leading to Ephraim, and whenever a fugitive from Ephraim would say, “Let me cross over,” the Gileadites would ask him, “Are you an Ephraimite?” If he answered, “No,” 6 they told him, “Please say Shibboleth.” If he said, “Sibboleth,” because he could not pronounce it correctly, they seized him and killed him at the fords of the Jordan. So at that time 42,000 Ephraimites were killed. 7 Jephthah judged Israel six years, and when he died, he was buried in one of the cities of Gilead.

context_lines: Victory over Ammon is followed by a conflict within Israel. Ephraim’s men accuse Jephthah of fighting without calling them and threaten to burn his house with him inside. He replies that he did call, that they failed to help, and that the LORD gave the victory when he risked his life. The exchange is no longer only about the earlier enemy; fellow Israelites now threaten one another.

Jephthah gathers Gilead’s men and fights Ephraim. The account also records the Ephraimites’ contemptuous description of the Gileadites as fugitives. That insult is not Jephthah’s own explanation of where the tribes live. It is part of the hostility that has developed between them.

The Gileadites control the Jordan crossings and use pronunciation to identify fugitives. The word שִׁבֹּלֶת, *shibboleth* (shih-BOH-leth), can mean a flowing stream, as [Brown–Driver–Briggs](https://biblehub.com/hebrew/7641.htm) notes for this verse. Those who say Sibboleth instead are seized and killed. The passage reports forty-two thousand Ephraimites killed in the conflict. A difference in speech has become a means of deciding who will live and who will die.

The notice then closes Jephthah’s story: he judges Israel for six years, dies, and is buried in Gilead. The rescue from a foreign enemy has been followed by devastating violence among the people themselves.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/judges/12.htm) reads the episode as a warning about pride, insulting labels, and rivalry over honor. He compares Ephraim’s complaint with its earlier confrontation with Gideon and urges believers to seek what makes for peace.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-book-of-judges/) notices the bitter reversal in the repeated word fugitives: those who used it to insult the Gileadites become fugitives themselves. He understands the death toll as covering the conflict, including battle, pursuit, and the crossings.
god_plan_lines: The divisions within Israel make the wider biblical purpose of reconciliation especially significant. [Ephesians 2:11–22](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/2.htm) describes Christ bringing together people once divided as Jews and Gentiles, reconciling them to God in one body through the cross and giving them access to the Father by one Spirit.

Paul then calls believers to humility, patience, love, and the preservation of that unity in peace ([Ephesians 4:1–6](https://biblehub.com/bsb/ephesians/4.htm)). The circumstances differ from Israel’s tribal conflict, but the direction is clear: God forms a people united in Christ, whose shared belonging is to shape how they live together.
